newsitem.title: USA: Judge denies tobacco class action in Castano spin off.
newsitem.headline: Judge denies tobacco class action in Castano spin off.

text.p: A federal judge in Pennsylvania has become the first to deny class-action status to a lawsuit spun off from a nationwide case brought on behalf of all smokers who say they are addicted to nicotine.

The ruling, issued late on Tuesday, applies to one of more than 20 class-action cases that were filed after last year's decertification of the massive Castano case, which would have created the largest group of plaintiffs in the nation's history.

In Castano, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans rejected the class action, saying the differences in state laws and the facts of individual cases were too great for class treatment on a nationwide basis. Instead, the court found that such suits would be better filed in state courts.
After that ruling, the group of some 60 plaintiffs lawyers involved in Castano began filing separate suits in individual states, including the one filed in Pennsylvania.

But U.S. District Judge Clarence Newcomer of Philadelphia ruled late Tuesday that the suit, Arch v. The American Tobacco Co., filed on behalf of more than 1 million Pennsylvania residents was also too broad.

"The reality of this litigation is that there are simply too many individual issues and class members to try this case efficiently. The manageability problems which would be encountered in litigating and trying this case are staggering," Newcomer wrote.
Major tobacco companies praised the ruling, saying it accepted the industry's legal position on attempts to use class actions to litigate smokers' claims.

"We expect this ruling will have strong persuasive effect in every other court where similar cases are pending," said John Mulderig, associate general counsel for New York-based Philip Morris Cos. Inc..

"The judicial systems was not designed to amalgamate large numbers of inherently individual claims at the expense of a defendant's constitutional right to a fair jury trial," said Gary Long, an attorney for Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. B&W, based in Louisville, Ky., is a unit of B.A.T Industries Plc.

Although cigarette makers said the ruling was a major victory, plaintiffs lawyers said that Newcomer's ruling had not given the industry everything it wanted and instead actually provided guidance on how to bring an acceptable case.
"He has not slammed the door," said Dianne Nast, one of the plaintiffs' lawyers. "He gave us instruction and we do intend to follow it."
She said the lawyers have several options but had not yet decided which one to take.

The Pennsylvania suit had been scheduled to be the first of the Castano spin-off cases to go to trial this fall. The Castano lawyers have brought at least 17 of the class actions filed since last year's appeals court decertification ruling.

Most of those suits apply to smokers in the states and in Puerto Rico where the individual cases are filed. However, just last month the group brought another broader case that would cover smokers in 35 states and the District of Columbia.
The suit, Clay v. American Tobacco Co., was filed in federal court in Benton, Ill. and was brought on behalf of plaintiffs who began smoking before the age of 18.
